query: Which material can be used for to improve the ductility and toughness of the HfZrTi high-entropy alloy (HEAs), and why?

generation.hypothesis: The addition of ductilizing elements, such as Ni or Co, to the HfZrTi high-entropy alloy (HEAs) can improve its ductility and toughness.
generation.intervention: addition of ductilizing elements (e.g., Ni or Co)
generation.structural_mediator: formation of solid solution with reduced brittleness
generation.mechanism: alloying elements reduce the alloy's brittleness and improve its overall mechanical behavior
generation.predicted_outcome: improved ductility and toughness of the HfZrTi HEA
generation.baseline: low ductility and toughness of the as-cast or wrought HfZrTi HEA
generation.uncertainty: effect of specific ductilizing elements and their concentrations on the mechanical properties of the HfZrTi HEA

cited_evidence.text:
Recently the concept of high-entropy alloys (HEAs), consisting of four or more principle metallic elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic ratios, has attracted considerable interest owing to its tendency to form solid solution with outstanding mechanical and functional properties [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. By introducing refractory elements including group IV (Ti, Zr, and Hf), V (V, Nb, and Ta), and VI (Cr, Mo, and W) in HEAs, the developed refractory HEAs (RHEAs) possess high melting temperature, outstanding strength and hardness, high thermal stability, and softening resistance at elevated temperatures, which opens up the possibilities of the alloy developments satisfying structural demands at high temperature.

Since the first WMoTaNb RHEA was reported in 2010, many literatures have been focused on the preparation methods and mechanical properties of RHEAs [ [7] , [8] ]. For example, the BCC WMoTaNb and WMoTaNbV HEAs maintained yield strength of 405 and 477 MPa at 1600 °C respectively, which were much higher than that of Inconel 718 and Haynes 230 [ [9] ]. However, most of these RHEAs are generally characterized with high density and poor high temperature oxidation

One of the most promising and progressive fields in modern material science is high-entropy alloys (HEAs). The first to propose HEAs’ concept was J.W. Yeh [ [1] ], but since then, it has changed rather significantly, especially during the last few years [ [2] ]. Due to their extremely high mechanical and physical properties, refractory HEAs are classified as a separate group of materials. Such alloying compositions mainly include elements from the IV, V, and VI columns of the periodic table with some additions of Al, Si, Ni, or Co [ [3] ].

First high-entropy equiatomic compositions based on refractory elements, such as NbMoTaW and NbMoTaWV, were obtained in prior research [ [4] , [5] ]. It was found that the alloys possess higher mechanical properties at higher temperatures in comparison to conventional superalloys, such as Inconel 718 and Haynes 230 [ [6] ]. It was also determined that the addition of V increases the hardness significantly (up to 11.4 GPa at 1150 °C) [ [7] ] and yield strength σ 0.2 from 1058 MPa to 1246 MPa [ [5] ]. On the other hand, these alloys are brittle at room temperature, leading to significant limitations of their application as structural materials. La

decision.trend: Research has been focused on improving the mechanical properties of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) through various processing techniques and alloy design. Earlier studies have explored the effects of composition, processing routes, and thermal treatments on the microstructure and properties of HEAs. Recently, there has been an emphasis on developing HEAs with improved ductility and toughness, particularly for high-temperature applications.
decision.unsolved: Despite progress in improving the mechanical properties of HEAs, the ductility and toughness of these alloys, especially at high temperatures, remain a significant challenge. The HfZrTi HEA, in particular, suffers from low ductility and toughness, which limits its potential applications.
decision.why: The next plausible step would be to investigate the effect of adding ductilizing elements, such as Ni or Co, to the HfZrTi HEA. This approach has been shown to improve the ductility and toughness of other HEAs, and could potentially enhance the properties of the HfZrTi alloy. The addition of these elements could help to reduce the alloy's brittleness and improve its overall mechanical behavior.
